confirmed: Source version is arXiv:2411.03295v5, dated 30 Jul 2025, with ACM publication formatting dated November 2025; the PDF has 33 pages. The title and four authors match the form (PDF p. 1). The complete markdown, including references and Appendix A, was read.
Appendix A is included on PDF pp. 30-33 and contains Tables 11-20, generation settings, prompts, and additional analyses; Table 8 is in the main text on PDF p. 18.

S4 is an online randomized between-subjects experiment: Prolific writers were randomly assigned to independent writing without external assistance or GPT-4 assistance rewriting their own drafts. This supports has_randomized_people_study=true and referral to the two-screener pipeline (PDF p. 10, section 3.2, Writing Task; p. 12, Participant Recruitment).

The writing sample of 103 is stated in the introduction and supported by Table 5 completed-writer counts of 52 US and 51 Indian participants, exceeding the 50-person threshold. Recruitment prose instead reports 52 Indian and 52 American recruits; the form correctly preserves this discrepancy and leaves the separately unreported randomization and arm-level people counts null (PDF p. 2, Phase 2 overview; p. 12, Table 5 and Participant Recruitment).

The 104 control and 102 HAI observations are comments, not arm-level participant counts. The abstract reports 600 participants across the paper, not 600 randomized writers (PDF p. 12, Participant Recruitment; p. 1, abstract).

S1 validation involved 230 MTurk annotators, with 142 US and 88 Indian annotators in Table 2; they annotated supplied comments rather than receiving AI writing assistance (PDF p. 7, Validating Argumentation Style; p. 9, Table 2).

S2 pilot country counts are US 27 and India 22; the form explicitly identifies 49 as their sum. This is below 50 people, but the pilot paragraph does not establish random assignment to AI writing assistance (PDF p. 10, section 3.1).

S3 reports 103 participants and four attention-check exclusions; Table 4 gives 50 US and 49 Indian evaluators, supporting the derived analyzed total of 99. Each evaluated four comment pairs, with randomized within-pair order, rather than producing AI-assisted writing (PDF pp. 9-10, Experiment 1 and Table 4).

S5 recruited 82 Indian and 82 US evaluators and reports 157 participants after seven attention-check exclusions, with 727 human evaluations. These counts and the stated four-pair protocol are reproduced as reported and kept separate from the writing sample (PDF p. 12, Human Evaluation of Constructiveness).

Writers responded to one homophobic and one Islamophobic thread, with a minimum of 50 words per final comment. The assisted condition required at least 20 draft words and at least one GPT-4 request, with options to accept, reject, regenerate, or edit suggestions; refinement is the appropriate AI role (PDF pp. 10-11, section 3.2 and Figure 2).

The relevant diversity analyses compare comments by different participants within each condition, matching thread and stance; they are not the initial-versus-final draft similarity analyses. This supports across_people and the pair unit for the three recorded similarity outcomes (PDF p. 17, section 4.2.3).

S4-O1 semantic similarity is control 0.41 versus HAI 0.42, and S4-O2 cosine similarity is control 0.33 versus HAI 0.30. Both statistics cells are dashes; the accompanying prose reports no significant difference using Mann-Whitney U tests with Bonferroni corrections (PDF p. 18, Table 8 and section 4.2.3).

S4-O3 ROUGE-L is control 0.18 versus HAI 0.16, with U=42029, Z=-3.73, p<0.001, r=0.16. Table 8 spells the row Rogue-L, while the prose says ROUGE-L; the form accurately records this and the lower overlap in HAI comments (PDF p. 18, Table 8 and section 4.2.3).

Every reported string and the one-line finding match Table 8, including the direction of each contrast and the absence of a significant semantic/cosine difference. No synthesis or pooled standardized estimate is reported; context_class=none is appropriate for the qualifying randomized diversity study (PDF pp. 10, 17-18).

The original short-form brief permits up to three main outcomes and explicitly requires core=unclear for referral when random assignment, at least 50 analyzed people, and an output-scored outcome are present. Thus the omission of the additional Distinct-2/TTR rows and the referral status do not require corrections (codex-jobs/lscreen-c906/brief.md, SHORT-form instructions; PDF pp. 10, 12, 18-19).

Ancillary fields were required to remain at defaults in the original short-form brief. In particular, company_involvement.any=false is an unfilled default, not a verified absence of company support: the PDF acknowledges Infosys and Cornell Global AI initiative (codex-jobs/lscreen-c906/brief.md, final form instructions; PDF p. 25, Acknowledgments).
summary: The form correctly identifies an online randomized writing experiment with 103 completed writers and output-scored diversity, requiring referral to the two-screener pipeline. The source version, participant counts, all three reported Table 8 results, and the one-line finding match the PDF, with no corrections needed to the required short-form fields.
